paragraphs.heading: What a histogram shows
paragraphs.text: A histogram is a picture of how quantitative data are distributed. To build one, you split the whole range of values into a series of intervals, called bins, and count how many values fall into each. The bins sit side by side without overlapping, and they are typically, though not necessarily, all the same size.

paragraphs.heading: Not a bar chart
paragraphs.text: Histograms are sometimes confused with bar charts. In a histogram each bin covers a different range of values, so together the bins show how the values are spread. In a bar chart each bar stands for a separate category, such as a different population, so the chart is used to compare categories. Some authors advise always leaving gaps between the bars of a bar chart to make clear it is not a histogram.

paragraphs.heading: Area tells the story
paragraphs.text: Strictly, a histogram uses rectangles whose widths are the class intervals and whose areas are proportional to the frequencies. The height of each rectangle is then the average frequency density over its interval. In one version, the area of each block equals the number of people in that category. In another, called a unit area histogram, each block's area is its fraction of the total, and all the areas add up to 1.

paragraphs.heading: Choosing the bins
paragraphs.text: No number of bins is the best one, and changing the bin size can bring out different features of the data. Wider bins where data points are sparse reduce noise from sampling randomness, while narrower bins where they are dense give more precise estimates, so varying the width within one histogram can help. Even so, equal-width bins are widely used. Trying several bin widths is a good way to learn more about the data.

paragraphs.heading: Reading the shape
paragraphs.text: People describe a histogram's pattern with words such as symmetric, skewed left or right, unimodal, bimodal or multimodal. A histogram offers a rough idea of how densely the data are spread and is often used to estimate the variable's probability density function. A smoother kernel density estimate will in general reflect that distribution more accurately. Histograms are still preferred when their statistical properties need modeling, since each bin varies independently and is simple to describe mathematically.

paragraphs.heading: Where the name comes from
paragraphs.text: Karl Pearson, the founder of mathematical statistics, introduced the word histogram in lectures at University College London in 1892. Pearson knew Ancient Greek well and built the word from ἱστός, meaning something set upright or a mast, pointing to the graph's vertical bars. The kind of graph was older than its name: the Scottish economist William Playfair used bar graphs for statistical measurements in his Commercial and political atlas of 1786.
